strong.text: Because his readers have been unsettled by teachers who left and claimed to speak for God, John tells them to test every spiritual claim rather than accept it. The reason he gives is that many false prophets have gone out into the world.

In light of the secession described earlier, the readers were vulnerable to persuasive teachers who claimed prophetic or spiritual authority. John therefore commands discernment: such claims must be examined rather than uncritically accepted. His stated rationale is the proliferation of false prophets in the world.

Reading this, I picture a church that has just been through a painful split. Some of the people who left are still talking about God and the Spirit very confidently, and it would be easy for the ones left behind to think 'well, they sound so sure, maybe they're right'. John steps in and says no, don't believe every spirit; examine them to see if they're really from God. The one reason he gives is that many false prophets have gone out into the world, so we should expect counterfeits and be careful.

John say do not believe every spirit. Maybe some people talk about God but they are not true. John gives the reason: there are many false prophets in the world. So the people must test the spirits and see if they come from God.

He is cautioning his readers not to take at face value every voice that claims inspiration. Counterfeit teachers, a great number of them, have set out among people, so each message has to be checked to see whether God is truly behind it.

John's reasoning is about protection. After people left their group and tried to win over those remaining, the believers needed a safeguard, and John gives them a habit: put every spiritual claim to the test, because false prophets are numerous in the world.

strong.text: John gives the testimony of three witnesses, the Spirit, the water and the blood, who all agree, and he argues that if we accept what people tell us, God's own testimony about his Son is even greater. They are good reasons because the witnesses agree with each other and because the ultimate witness is God himself, who can't be wrong.

John offers a threefold testimony in agreement, namely the Spirit, the water and the blood, and then reasons from the lesser to the greater: if human testimony is customarily accepted, divine testimony carries far more weight. These grounds are compelling because the witnesses are consistent and because the highest possible authority, God himself, stands behind them.

The way I read it, John doesn't just say 'believe me'. He lines up witnesses: the Spirit, the water and the blood, and they don't contradict one another. Then he uses an everyday argument: we accept what people tell us in court and in ordinary life, so how much more should we accept what God himself says about his Son. For me these are good reasons because there's more than one witness, they're unanimous, and the person vouching for Jesus is God, who is the most reliable witness there could ever be.

John say there are three witnesses: the Spirit, the water and the blood. They all agree together. Also, we believe what people say, so we must believe what God says more, because God is greater. This is a good reason because God never lies and three witnesses are saying the same.

He cites a trio of corroborating voices (the Spirit, baptism and the cross, as most take it) who tell one consistent story, and he adds that since we routinely trust a person's word, the declaration of the Almighty should outweigh it. That is persuasive: consistent evidence, backed by the ultimate authority.

I'd focus on the legal idea behind it: in the Old Testament you needed two or three witnesses to prove something, and John supplies three. His second reason is the step from human witnesses to God's own: if people's testimony is accepted, God's is better. The reasons are good because they meet the legal standard and rest on God's own character as truthful.
